title: If You Want Your Team to Be More Productive, Consider Trying a New Periodization
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author introduces periodization as a leadership lever: changing the time intervals by which a team sets goals and measures progress. Most organizations run on conventional rhythms such as monthly updates, quarterly deadlines and annual reviews, and people orient their effort around those checkpoints. The post suggests that deliberately shortening or reshaping these periods, for example weekly rather than monthly sales check-ins, can shake up engagement and output. Such changes can be temporary experiments rather than permanent policy. The underlying claim is that time conventions are more fluid than leaders assume, and that new measuring periods change how people think and work.
points: Regular reporting intervals shape behavior, for instance pushing people to book revenue before a monthly update.
Shortening a traditional timeframe is presented as a way to raise engagement and activity.
Periodization changes can be tried temporarily, which lowers the risk of experimenting.
Time traditions resist change, so leaders need creativity and judgment in deciding where a new interval might help.
quotes: Performance reviews, earnings calls, forecasts, training milestones, strategy updates, team meetings, project planning, and numerous other activities typically occur at regular intervals. Leaders depend on the structured time commitments to promote execution and results.

For instance, a monthly sales or revenue update pushes team members to book revenue before the update meeting so it is recognized, rewarded, and counted against their goals. Monthly or quarterly deadlines are common timeframes for many of an organization's most important milestones and progress reports.

In many instances, simply shortening a traditional timeframe dramatically shakes things up and produces a different level of engagement and production. Leaders sometimes make these changes temporary instead of permanent.

Creativity and common sense are the primary guides for thinking about how to incorporate periodization into the workplace. Time traditions are highly resistant to change, but leaders who occasionally introduce new periods often reap significant benefits.
How we choose to count and measure time is more fluid than most leaders think. And changes in time periods get people thinking and working differently.
